newsitem.title: USA: America Online offers refunds in settlement.
newsitem.headline: America Online offers refunds in settlement.

text.p: America Online Inc., besieged by complaints by frustrated customers unable to log on and facing the threat of lawsuits by dozens of states, agreed Wednesday to give refunds.

The world's largest online computer service, with 8 million subscribers, agreed in principle to give customers their choice of a free month online or up to $39.90 -- the cost of two months of the service -- Illinois Attorney General Jim Ryan told a news conference.

America Online, which since Dec. 1 has been struggling to deal with an unexpectedly big upsurge in the number of subscribers, also agreed to halt for a month advertising aimed at attracting new customers.
Ryan said he expected the Dulles, Va.-based company would formally sign the agreement by Thursday.
"We're comfortable with it. We think it's a good deal for consumers," he said.
The proposed settlement headed off, for now, consumer fraud lawsuits threatened by prosecutors from 36 states, including California, New York and Illinois.
The agreement calls for customers to receive graduated refunds of up to $39.90 based on how much time they spent over the past two months logged onto AOL, Ryan said.
Any customer can demand a free month's service, no questions asked, he said.

America Online Chief Executive Officer Steve Case declined to estimate the cost of the refunds, but New York state Attorney General Dennis Vacco told a Manhattan news conference he expected the refunds will cost the company several million dollars in his state alone.
Ryan said the pact originally covered 37 states, but said Missouri's attorney general backed out at the last minute to take a closer look at the proposed refunds.
AOL ran into capacity troubles after it switched its customers from a subscription plan based on the number of hours online to a flat $19.95 monthly rate for unlimited access.

Under the agreement announced Wednesday, AOL agreed to cease all new advertising for the month of February unless already contracted for. Vacco said any ads must include a disclaimer that on-line traffic jams may prevent customers from getting online.
The prosecutors had complained America Online was continuing to advertise and sign up new customers even as it could not deliver the service to existing users.
AOL also agreed to hire additional operators to field calls from customers seeking to cancel the service, and will set up facilities to accept faxed or online cancellation requests.
Customers in the 36 states could also contact the attorney general's office in that state to file a refund request.
"If there are fresh complaints, we can still file a lawsuit under the consumer fraud laws," Ryan said. "This does not preclude us from acting on behalf of consumers."
The company must provide each state's attorney general with compliance statements about progress of the programme within 15 days of signing the agreement, Ryan said.

"We are fairly assured that they are adding capacity," he said, reiterating promises from America Online that it would expand the service so that customers would not be frustrated by busy signals when trying to log on from their computers.
"America Online was quick to come to the table to try to resolve this," Ryan said.
Attorneys general or their aides from 20 states met last week in Chicago with the company.
Under the graduated refund plan, customers who spent less than two hours on the service in either December or January could receive the full $39.90 refund.

If more than two hours but less than eight hours was spent signed on, customers could get a 50 percent refund. Customers logged on for between eight and 15 hours were entitled to a 25 percent refund. Beyond 15 hours, no refund would be offered.
